raw_case_text:
We present a case of a 53-year-old man who came to our department for a large multinodular goiter with multiple suspicious nodules on ultrasound. The diagnosis was made in 1999 during hospitalization for an episode of thyrotoxicosis. The patient was diagnosed as HIV-positive in 1994 and began antiretroviral treatment with AZT (zidovudine) and Ddi (didanosine) with minimal initial benefit; however, subsequent worsening of the immunological condition was noted. Therefore, beginning in June 1997, therapy was switched to d4T (stavudine) plus 3TC (lamivudine) and IDV (indinavir); this achieved excellent viral replication control and improved the immunological condition. In 1999, a change in HIV treatment was necessary due to the presence of an important lipid dysmetabolism with hypertriglyceridemia, modification of the habitus with an important lipohypertrophy of the cervicodorsal region (buffalo hump and taurine neck) and loss of subcutaneous fat of the legs (Fig. 1A-D). Therapy with AZT (zidovudine)+ 3TC (lamivudine) + EFV (efavirenz) enabled control of viral replication and stability of the lipodystrophic picture. The patient had undergone multiple liposuctions, but they were not effective, likely due to the excessive accumulation of adipose tissue. In our opinion, the most relevant clinical aspect to consider was the large buffalo hump and taurine neck due to lipodystrophy. He also presented with negative thyroid autoimmunity, with normal calcitonin and calcemic blood values. The ultrasound exam showed struma with partial retrosternal engagement and multiple thyroid nodules increasing in size relative to a previous check, as well as suspicious features for neoplasia. The patient had undergone several needle aspirations, which failed due to the thickness and abundancy of the adipose tissue.
Patient comorbidities were mainly based on the alteration of glucose metabolism (due to diabetes mellitus), alteration of bone metabolism (due to osteopenia), severe obesity (body mass index, BMI, of 34.6), and hypertension, as well as slight limitation in running, weightlifting and playing intense sports. He also reported that a previous HCV hepatopathy had been treated with Harvoni. The indication to remove the thyroid glands was suggested by the patient's endocrinologist, primarily due to the suspicious nodules. Preoperative anesthesia evaluation predicted an American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) anesthetic risk of 3, requiring complex intubation for the patient's habitus and for the shrinkage of the trachea. Indeed, preoperative chest X-ray showed an ovalization of the tracheal lumen (11 mm) to a plane passing through C7 (Fig. 2).
After careful positioning (Fig. 3A and B), the patient underwent total thyroidectomy by anterior cervicotomy. Total thyroidectomy was performed with technical difficulties: first, intubation of the patient was required for the operation due to the hyperextension of the neck; second, access to the goiter was difficult due to the amount of adipose tissue, as well as the buffalo hump and taurine neck. Thyroid isolation was complicated on the right side of the gland for the increased volume, particularly due to difficulty in recurring laryngeal nerve isolation. No intraoperative complications and no bleeding loss were observed during or after surgery. The drains were removed on the second postoperative day. Despite the patient's HIV infection, no complications were noted after surgery, especially around the wound. Calcium blood values stayed in the normal range after surgery. The patient presented with dysphonia; therefore, direct laryngoscopy was performed, which showed fixation of the right vocal string with good phonatory compensation, as well as consistency of the respiratory space. Therefore, the patient was sent to logopedic rehabilitation after discharge from the hospital.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 53-year-old male presenting for surgical evaluation and management of a large multinodular goiter with multiple suspicious thyroid nodules and severe cervicodorsal lipodystrophy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 53-year-old male was evaluated for surgical management of a long-standing large multinodular goiter, first diagnosed in 1999 during an admission for thyrotoxicosis. Serial ultrasonography demonstrated enlarging thyroid nodules with suspicious neoplastic features and retrosternal engagement. Multiple prior fine needle aspiration attempts had failed due to excessive cervical adipose tissue. The patient also experienced progressive dysmorphic changes including cervicodorsal lipohypertrophy ('buffalo hump' and 'taurine neck') and peripheral fat loss refractory to multiple liposuctions.
subjective.past_medical_history: Underlying chronic viral condition managed with long-term antiretroviral therapy (initially zidovudine and didanosine in 1994, switched to stavudine, lamivudine, and indinavir in 1997, and subsequently transitioned in 1999 to zidovudine, lamivudine, and efavirenz due to severe antiretroviral-associated lipodystrophy and hypertriglyceridemia); history of thyrotoxicosis (1999); diabetes mellitus; osteopenia; severe obesity (BMI 34.6 kg/m2); hypertension; chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) hepatopathy successfully treated with ledipasvir/sofosbuvir (Harvoni); multiple prior liposuctions.
subjective.review_of_systems: Dysphonia postoperatively; slight functional limitation in running, weightlifting, and intense sports; denies acute compressive airway obstruction symptoms preoperatively.

objective.physical_examination: Physical habitus: Severe obesity (BMI 34.6 kg/m2); massive cervicodorsal lipohypertrophy ('buffalo hump' and 'taurine neck') with loss of subcutaneous adipose tissue in the lower extremities. Neck: Marked adipose accumulation, large multinodular goiter palpable. Preoperative ASA class 3. Postoperative direct laryngoscopy: Fixation of the right vocal cord with good phonatory compensation and preserved respiratory space.
objective.routine_investigations: Laboratory studies: Thyroid autoimmunity negative; serum calcitonin and calcium levels within normal limits preoperatively and postoperatively. Preoperative chest X-ray: Tracheal compression with ovalization of tracheal lumen (11 mm) at C7 plane.
objective.advanced_workup: Neck ultrasound: Struma with partial retrosternal extension and multiple thyroid nodules increasing in size with suspicious features for neoplasia. Multiple failed fine-needle aspirations. Direct laryngoscopy: Right vocal cord paresis/fixation.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Large multinodular goiter with retrosternal engagement and suspicious features for neoplasia, complicated by severe antiretroviral-induced lipodystrophy syndrome (taurine neck, buffalo hump, peripheral lipoatrophy, hypertriglyceridemia) in a patient with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV; diagnosed 1994, virologically controlled on zidovudine, lamivudine, and efavirenz), diabetes mellitus, osteopenia, hypertension, and treated hepatitis C.
Surgical Management & Outcome: Patient underwent total thyroidectomy via anterior cervicotomy; procedure was technically challenging due to difficult airway intubation, excessive adipose tissue, and difficult right recurrent laryngeal nerve isolation. Surgical drains were removed on postoperative day 2 without hematoma or wound infection. Postoperative right vocal cord palsy was documented on direct laryngoscopy, managed with logopedic speech rehabilitation following discharge.
